filename: Representing subgrid-scale cloud effects in a radiation parameterization using machine learning_ MLE-radiation v1.0
title: Representing subgrid-scale cloud effects in a radiation parameterization using machine learning: MLe-radiation v1.0
parameterization_target: cloud radiative impact on shortwave and longwave heating rates
code_availability: The software code for the ICON model is available at https://doi.org/10.35089/WDCC/IconRelease01 under the BSD-3C license. The exact version for high-resolution simulations is icon-2024.10 and for coarse-resolution, version 2.6.4 is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18853569. The pyRTE+RRTMGP front-end code is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16644555. Training and plotting code is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17280639.
testbed_rationale: High-resolution global storm-resolving simulation data (coarse-grained to ESM grid) paired with radiative transfer baseline calculations are publicly available on Zenodo along with complete open-source training and evaluation code, making it an ideal testbed for subgrid cloud radiative parameterization.
pain_points: Formula differences in converting radiative flux divergence to heating rates (cv vs. cp) between model versions caused massive initial biases (up to 10 K/day) that required scaling.
Global storm-resolving resolution of 5 km remains too coarse to resolve shallow convection, leaving planetary boundary layer cloud radiative effects partially unresolved.
Offline evaluation only; stability and coupling performance in an active GCM run remain to be tested.
Aerosols and spatially varying trace gases were omitted from the high-resolution run, preventing direct learning of secondary radiative interactions.
Grid mismatch and elevation discrepancies over complex terrain caused by rotated/shifted coarse grid required discarding misaligned cells.
extraction_notes: The ML model (MLe-radiation v1.0) predicts only the cloud radiative impact (CRI) residual heating rates, which are added to physics-calculated clear-sky heating rates computed with pyRTE (RTE+RRTMGP). The evaluation is entirely offline against coarse-grained QUBICC data.
